title: Our research in one minute
text:
Research on inequality should reach everyone, not only specialists. Each of these one-minute videos explains an article of the team in plain language: the question, how it was answered, what was found, a key result shown as a figure and why it matters for society. You can share them freely on social networks, in classes or in public talks, citing GiniUs. Videos of articles on water services or survey methods also explain their link with inequality. Each video shows the quality indicators of the journal: JCR quartile in the year of publication and, where applicable, rating in the Chartered ABS Academic Journal Guide.

A practical guide to proper estimation and inference of the Gini index by avoiding often encountered methodological pitfalls

J.F. Muñoz, J.M. Pavía and E. Álvarez-Verdejo · Social Indicators Research (2026) · JCR Q1 · doi.org/10.1007/s11205-026-03831-x

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. The Gini index is the most used measure of inequality. But computing it from data is error-prone. Do common practices give wrong numbers and wrong margins of error?
What they found. Some widely used formulas give inaccurate estimates of inequality. A popular regression-based method seriously underestimates the margin of error when incomes are very skewed and unequal. Jackknife methods give the most accurate margins of error.
Key result (in the video). How often the 95% margin of error contains the true Gini. Monte Carlo illustration: lognormal incomes, samples of 100, 4,000 replications (computed by GiniUs). As inequality grows, the regression method falls far below 95%.
Why it matters. Margins of error that are too small can make us believe inequality changed when it did not. The paper gives practical recommendations and the free R package giniVarCI.
Download the video (MP4)




Exploring and correcting the bias in the estimation of the Gini measure of inequality

J.F. Muñoz, P.J. Moya-Fernández and E. Álvarez-Verdejo · Sociological Methods & Research (2025) · JCR Q1 · doi.org/10.1177/00491241231176847

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. There are many formulas to estimate the Gini index from a sample. Do they all give the right answer?
What they found. One popular formula strongly overestimates inequality when inequality is low. With skewed and unequal data, the usual estimators tend to underestimate inequality. Bootstrap and jackknife corrections reduce the bias, and a simple criterion tells when to use them.
Key result (in the video). Relative bias (%) of three common Gini formulas. Monte Carlo illustration with the paper’s estimators: lognormal incomes, samples of 20 people, 20,000 replications (computed by GiniUs).
Why it matters. Differences in inequality between countries, regions or groups can come from the formula used, not from real differences. Choosing the right estimator avoids wrong conclusions.
Download the video (MP4)




The “Happy and Poor” paradox: why do some poor people report being very happy?

J. Guardiola, F. García-Quero and A. García-García · Applied Research in Quality of Life (2026) · JCR Q1 · doi.org/10.1007/s11482-026-10637-z

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. Many people living in poverty say they are very happy. How can that be?
Six explanations. Their basic needs are met and they are satisfied in key areas of life; they adapt to hardship and have modest aspirations. Scientists and policymakers may misjudge how well they are doing. Their culture supports happiness, and maldevelopment has not eroded it.
The idea in one picture (in the video). Income and life satisfaction. Conceptual illustration. The study explains why some poor people are in the top-left corner.
Why it matters. Poverty is not only a lack of income. Listening to how people evaluate their own lives helps design better development policies.
Download the video (MP4)




Does economic growth drive equitable water and sanitation access? Assessing inequality reduction across 64 nations

M. García-López, S. López-Ruiz and G. Cuadrado-Quesada · Sustainable Development (2026) · JCR Q1 · doi.org/10.1002/sd.70894

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. When a country grows richer, does access to water and sanitation become more equal?
What they found. Growth improves access overall, but the poorest and rural populations are left behind. Inequality in sanitation is not related to growth. Unequal access to water also holds back GDP per capita.
Key result (in the video). What economic growth does, and does not do, for water and sanitation. Source: Sustainable Development (2026), 64 countries.
Why it matters. Growth alone will not deliver water and sanitation for all (SDG 6). Effective governance and efficient water use are needed.
Download the video (MP4)




Does tourism reduce socio-economic inequality? Insights from the pandemic based on space and time models for the EU

C.M. Llorca-Rodríguez, R.M. García-Fernández and J. Chica-Olmo · Economia Politica (2026) · JCR Q2 · doi.org/10.1007/s40888-025-00390-1

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. Does tourism help to reduce poverty and social exclusion in European regions?
What they found. International (inbound) tourism increases poverty and social exclusion in destination regions. Domestic tourism reduces them, in destinations and in neighbouring regions. Some other effects are statistically significant but economically very small.
Key result (in the video). Effect of tourism on the risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE). Source: Economia Politica (2026), EU regions. The inverted-U link of total tourism is negligible in practice.
Why it matters. Tourism does not reduce poverty by itself. Market structures, labour regulation, competitiveness and social protection decide who benefits.
Download the video (MP4)




Dynamic spatio-temporal modelling of tourism impact on income inequality and polarization: inbound and domestic flows in the EU

C.M. Llorca-Rodríguez, A.C. Casas-Jurado, R.M. García-Fernández and J. Chica-Olmo · Papers in Regional Science (2025) · JCR Q2 · ABS 3 · doi.org/10.1016/j.pirs.2025.100122

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. Does tourism make income more equal in European regions, or less?
What they found. Overall, tourism and inequality follow an inverted-U shape. Inbound tourism increases inequality and polarization in destinations; domestic tourism reduces them. Both types improve the income distribution of neighbouring regions.
Key result (in the video). Effect of tourism on income inequality and polarization. Source: Papers in Regional Science (2025), EU NUTS-1 regions. Overall, tourism and inequality follow an inverted-U shape.
Why it matters. Useful for the EU Cohesion Policy: domestic tourism supports cohesion, and social protection (education, health, unemployment and retirement) should be strengthened.
Download the video (MP4)




Inequalities in talents’ earnings: a tale of two European countries

T. Addabbo and C. Mussida · Social Indicators Research (2025) · JCR Q1 · doi.org/10.1007/s11205-025-03692-w

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. Are young graduates paid differently in Italy and in Germany? And are women paid less than men?
What they found. The wage gap against Italian talents grew in 2022, mainly because the same qualifications are paid less. The gap grew more for women, especially at the top. Gender gap among talents: Italy from 10% to 22.5%; Germany from 27.5% to 15%.
Key result (in the video). Gender pay gap among young talents. Source: Social Indicators Research (2025). In Italy the gap more than doubled; in Germany it almost halved.
Why it matters. Better pay and conditions in Germany help explain why young Italian talents move there. Policies are needed to attract and keep talent.
Download the video (MP4)




Innovation and poverty-related income gaps in Europe: evidence from the North–South divide

P.A. Cano-Chica, V.E. Yáñez-Justicia, A. Rodríguez-Copete, E. Álvarez-Verdejo and A.J. López-Montoya · Journal of Poverty (2026) · JCR Q3 · doi.org/10.1080/10875549.2026.2671664

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. How are innovation and entrepreneurship related to the income gaps that affect the poorest households in Europe?
What the study analyses. How innovation dynamics interact with income inequality and poverty-related vulnerability. Differences between Northern and Southern Europe. Changes within countries over time and differences between countries.
What the study compares (in the video). Innovation, income gaps and poverty in Europe. Source: Journal of Poverty (2026). Results by country and over time in the article.
Why it matters. Innovation policies can widen or narrow income gaps. Knowing where and how helps to design fairer innovation policies in Europe.
Download the video (MP4)




Changing prices after the reform of local public services: remunicipalization versus privatization

D. Albalate, G. Bel, F. González-Gómez, J.C. Hernández-Gutiérrez and A.J. Picazo-Tadeo · Journal of Regulatory Economics (2024) · JCR Q3 · doi.org/10.1007/s11149-024-09472-7

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. When a town takes its water service back from a private company, or hands it over to one, what happens to the water bill?
What they found. Remunicipalization showed smaller price increases than privatization. But that gap came from a few towns with abnormally low prices before the reform. Once these towns are accounted for, the type of reform makes no difference to prices.
Key result (in the video). What happened to water prices after the reform. Source: Journal of Regulatory Economics (2024), Spanish municipalities.
Why it matters. Decisions about who runs public services should rest on evidence about what citizens pay, not only on ideology.
Link with inequality. Water bills weigh more on low-income households. Knowing what drives water prices helps protect affordability and the human right to water.
Download the video (MP4)




Pro-environmental behaviour in household water use. A gender perspective

L. Granda, P.J. Moya-Fernández, R.M. Soriano-Miras and F. González-Gómez · Sustainable Water Resources Management (2024) · doi.org/10.1007/s40899-023-01027-6

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. Do women and men save water at home in the same way?
What they found. There is no gender gap in the number of water-saving habits. But there are differences in specific habits. They follow how household chores are shared: tasks traditionally done by women or by men.
Key result (in the video). Saving water at home: women and men. Source: Sustainable Water Resources Management (2024), ten household water uses.
Why it matters. Water-saving campaigns work better when they reach the person who actually does each household task.
Link with inequality. Gender inequality in sharing household chores also shapes who carries the effort of saving water at home.
Download the video (MP4)




Challenges of Urban Water Cycle Management in Small Spanish Municipalities: The Case of the Province of Granada

F.J. García-Martínez, F. Osorio and F. González-Gómez · Water (2025) · JCR Q2 · doi.org/10.3390/w17121750

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. Do people in small villages get the same water services as people in cities?
What they found. Water management in Spain shows two very different realities: populated areas and small towns. Small municipalities face specific problems in managing the urban water cycle. Recommendations: create optimal service areas and an independent regulatory body.
Key result (in the video). Two realities of water management, and what to do. Source: Water (2025), province of Granada (Spain).
Why it matters. Better organisation and regulation can bring rural water services closer to urban standards.
Link with inequality. Territorial inequality: whether you live in a city or a village should not decide the quality of your water service.
Download the video (MP4)




Unconditional variance estimation under complex surveys

Y.G. Berger · International Statistical Review (2025) · JCR Q1 · doi.org/10.1111/insr.70001

Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Download the video.
The question. How precise are the figures we get from large official surveys?
What they found. The margin of error can be computed without complex correction terms. The estimator is simple and asymptotically unbiased under stratified, multistage and informative designs. It also gives hypothesis tests and works under ordered systematic sampling.
Key result (in the video). A simpler way to get the margin of error. Source: International Statistical Review (2025).
Why it matters. Simple and reliable margins of error make it easier to use survey data correctly.
Link with inequality. Inequality and poverty are measured with complex surveys such as EU-SILC. Reliable margins of error tell us whether a change in inequality is real.
Download the video (MP4)

title: The R package giniVarCI
text: giniVarCI is the open-source R package developed in GiniUs (objective OG3). It is available on CRAN and on R-universe, where it can also be used in the browser with webR (see the R exercises).

title: The R package giniVarCI
text:
What it does

Estimates the Gini index for samples from infinite populations (igini(), iginindex()) and from finite populations with survey weights or inclusion probabilities (fgini(), fginindex()), with the different expressions of the literature.
Computes variances and confidence intervals with different methods: percentile and BCa bootstrap, jackknife, linearisation and empirical likelihood (igini(), fgini()), and compares them (icompareCI(), fcompareCI()).
Computes the Gini index of continuous probability distributions (Beta, Burr, chi-squared, Dagum, F, Fisk, Gamma, Gompertz, lognormal, Pareto, etc.: functions gbeta(), gdagum(), ggamma(), …).
Draws samples with a Gini index set by the user (gsample()), very useful for simulation studies.
Uses Rcpp (C++), so calculations are faster than in other packages that compute the Gini index.

title: The R package giniVarCI
text:
Installation
install.packages("giniVarCI")            # from CRAN
library(giniVarCI)
vignette("GiniVarInterval", package = "giniVarCI")

title: The R package giniVarCI
text:
Examples
Infinite populations.
set.seed(123)
y <- gsample(n = 100, gini = 0.5, distribution = "lognormal")

igini(y)                             # Gini index (with bias correction)
iginindex(y, method = 5)             # a specific expression of the Gini index
igini(y, interval = "zjackknife")    # jackknife interval
igini(y, interval = "BCa")           # BCa bootstrap interval
igini(y, interval = "ELchisq")       # empirical likelihood interval
icompareCI(y, plotCI = TRUE)         # compares all the intervals
Intervals available in igini(): "pbootstrap", "BCa", "zjackknife", "tjackknife", "zalinearization", "zblinearization", "talinearization", "tblinearization", "ELchisq" and "ELboot".
Finite populations (survey data).
data(eusilc, package = "laeken")
y <- eusilc$eqIncome[eusilc$db040 == "Burgenland"]
w <- eusilc$rb050[eusilc$db040 == "Burgenland"]

fgini(y, w)                                    # weighted Gini index
fginindex(y, w, method = 3)                    # Berger (2008), mid-point distribution function
fgini(y, w, interval = "zjackknife")           # jackknife interval
fgini(y, w, interval = "zalinearization")      # linearisation interval
Methods available in fginindex(): 1, Langel and Tillé (2013); 2 (default), Alfons and Templ (2012) and Langel and Tillé (2013); 3, Berger (2008); 4, Berger and Gedik-Balay (2020); 5, Lerman and Yitzhaki (1989).

text: This page summarises the main results of the project. It is updated as new articles are published; the full list is in Publications. The main articles are also explained in plain language in one-minute videos, and the evidence of their impact (open access, citations, online attention and use) is on the Impact page.

title: Results and conclusions
section: OG1 · The bias of the Gini index
text:
OG1 · The bias of the Gini index






✔ Objective achieved. The four specific objectives of OG1 (OE1–OE4) have been completed: the expressions of the Gini index have been classified, the scenarios with large biases identified, bias-correction techniques (bootstrap and jackknife) proposed, and a practical criterion for applied users established. The results are published in Sociological Methods & Research (2025) and Social Indicators Research (2026) and implemented in the R package giniVarCI.



Results. Monte Carlo studies with six distributions (Pareto, Dagum with p=20 and p=0.5, lognormal, Weibull and Gamma), Gini indices from 0.1 to 0.8 and different sample sizes. They can be reproduced with the interactive bias explorer.
Conclusions.

\widehat{G}_n^{a} has excessively large biases in datasets with low inequality. Two equivalent solutions:

replace \widehat{F}_n(t) with the smoothed (mid-point) distribution function \widehat{F}_n^{*}(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in S}\left[\delta(y_i<t)+0.5\,\delta(y_i=t)\right], which gives the estimator \widehat{G}_n^{b};
subtract 1/n when there are no ties: \widehat{G}_n^{b}=\widehat{G}_n^{a}-1/n.

Skewness has a significant effect on the bias of the three versions of the Gini index (hypothesis H1).
In highly skewed distributions, inequality has a major effect on the bias of the three versions (hypothesis H2).

Publications. Exploring and correcting the bias in the estimation of the Gini measure of inequality (Muñoz, Moya-Fernández and Álvarez-Verdejo, Sociological Methods & Research); A practical guide to proper estimation and inference of the Gini index by avoiding often encountered methodological pitfalls (Social Indicators Research, 2026).

set.seed(1)
y <- rlnorm(500, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 0.8)   # lognormal incomes
y <- sort(y)

section: Exercise 3. The bias of the estimators: a small simulation
text:
Exercise 3. The bias of the estimators: a small simulation
For a lognormal distribution, the true Gini index is G = 2\Phi(\sigma/\sqrt{2}) - 1. Compare the average of the three estimators with the true value.

set.seed(123)
G     <- 0.1                              # true Gini index: try 0.1, 0.4 and 0.8
sigma <- sqrt(2) * qnorm((G + 1) / 2)     # lognormal parameter with this Gini index
n     <- 50                               # try 20, 50 and 500

est <- replicate(2000, { y <- rlnorm(n, 0, sigma); c(Ga = gini_a(y), Gb = gini_b(y), Gc = gini_c(y)) })
RB  <- 100 * (rowMeans(est) - G) / G       # relative bias (%)
round(RB, 2)

boxplot(t(est), col = c("#D43F3A", "#1A5FA8", "#C9962B"), ylab = "Estimates",
        main = paste("G =", G, "  n =", n))
abline(h = G, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
▶ RunResetCtrl/Cmd + Enter

section: Exercise 4. Jackknife standard error and confidence interval
text:
Exercise 4. Jackknife standard error and confidence interval

set.seed(2)
y <- rlnorm(100, 0, 1)
n <- length(y)

G_hat <- gini_c(y)
G_loo <- sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) gini_c(y[-i]))   # leave-one-out estimates

bias <- (n - 1) * (mean(G_loo) - G_hat)
se   <- sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((G_loo - mean(G_loo))^2))

c(estimate = G_hat, bias = bias, se = se,
  ci_lower = G_hat - 1.96 * se, ci_upper = G_hat + 1.96 * se,
  true_G = 2 * pnorm(1 / sqrt(2)) - 1)
▶ RunResetCtrl/Cmd + Enter


Question. Is the true value inside the interval? The calculator applies the same method to your own data.

title: Try it in R
section: Exercise 5. Missing data: MCAR versus MNAR
text:
Exercise 5. Missing data: MCAR versus MNAR
Delete 30% of the incomes completely at random (MCAR), or delete them more often among the richest (MNAR), and compare complete-case analysis with mean imputation.

set.seed(3)
n <- 1000
y <- rlnorm(n, 0, 0.8)
G_full <- gini_c(y)

# MCAR: every unit has a 30% probability of not responding
miss_mcar <- runif(n) < 0.30
# MNAR: the probability of not responding grows with income (30% on average)
p <- plogis(-1.2 + 1.5 * as.numeric(scale(log(y))))
miss_mnar <- runif(n) < p

complete <- function(miss) gini_c(y[!miss])
mean_imp <- function(miss) { z <- y; z[miss] <- mean(y[!miss]); gini_c(z) }

round(rbind(
  MCAR = c(missing = mean(miss_mcar), complete_cases = complete(miss_mcar), mean_imputation = mean_imp(miss_mcar)),
  MNAR = c(missing = mean(miss_mnar), complete_cases = complete(miss_mnar), mean_imputation = mean_imp(miss_mnar))), 3)
c(Gini_full_sample = G_full)
▶ RunResetCtrl/Cmd + Enter


Question. Which method works under MCAR? What happens under MNAR? The missing data simulator compares more methods, including multiple imputation.

title: The Gini index: definition and estimation
text:
Definitions
Let Y be a non-negative continuous random variable with distribution function F_Y and mean \mu_Y = E[Y]=\int_0^{\infty} y\,dF_Y(y). The Gini index has several equivalent definitions.
Definition 1 (Lorenz, 1905; Langel and Tillé, 2013). Twice the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve L_\alpha: 
G = 2\left(0.5 - \int_{0}^{1} L_{\alpha}\, d\alpha \right), \qquad
L_{\alpha} = \frac{1}{\mu_{Y}}\int_{0}^{Y_{\alpha}}y\,dF_{Y}(y)=\frac{1}{\mu_{Y}}\int_{0}^{\alpha}Y_{u}\,du,
 where Y_{\alpha}=F_{Y}^{-1}(\alpha)=\inf\{t:F_{Y}(t)\geq \alpha\} is the \alpha-quantile of Y.
Definition 2 (Kendall and Stuart, 1977). Half the relative mean absolute difference: 
G = \frac{D_{G}}{2 \mu_{Y}}, \qquad D_{G}=E|X-Y|=\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{0}^{\infty} |x-y|\,dF_{Y}(x)\,dF_{Y}(y).

Definition 3 (Qin et al., 2010; Berger and Gedik-Balay, 2020): 
G=\frac{1}{\mu_{Y}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\{2F_{Y}(y)-1\}\,y\,dF_{Y}(y)=1 - \frac{1}{\mu_{Y}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\{1-F_{Y}(y)\}^{2}dy.

Definition 4 (Anand, 1983; Lerman and Yitzhaki, 1984): 
G=\frac{2}{\mu_{Y}}\,\mathrm{cov}\{Y, F_{Y}(Y)\}.

Definition 5 (Yitzhaki, 1998; Peng, 2011; Berger and Gedik-Balay, 2020): 
G=1 - \frac{\mu_{Z}}{\mu_{Y}}, \qquad \mu_{Z} = E(Z)= \int_{0}^{\infty}\{1-F_{Z}(z)\}\,dz,
 where Z=\min\{Y_{a}, Y_{b}\} and Y_{a}, Y_{b} are independent copies of Y.






All these estimators, with variances and confidence intervals, are implemented in the R package giniVarCI, developed in this project: install.packages("giniVarCI").

title: The Gini index: definition and estimation
text:
Estimation in infinite populations
We use a sample of size n=50 from a Pareto distribution. The R functions below are written in base R so that they can be read and checked easily; giniVarCI computes them much faster with C++ code.

# Sample selection (Pareto distribution with scale 1 and shape 1.5, by inversion)
set.seed(123)
rpareto_base <- function(n, scale = 1, shape) scale / runif(n)^(1 / shape)
Y.n <- rpareto_base(n = 50, shape = 1.5)
round(Y.n, 3)

 [1]  2.295  1.172  1.815  1.086  1.042  7.840  1.531  1.079  1.487  1.686
[11]  1.030  1.695  1.296  1.450  4.553  1.073  2.546  8.268  2.103  1.032
[21]  1.081  1.277  1.346  1.004  1.325  1.258  1.500  1.415  2.287  3.588
[31]  1.025  1.071  1.280  1.165 11.818  1.636  1.202  2.774  2.146  2.651
[41]  3.660  1.799  1.801  1.944  3.504  3.730  2.641  1.664  2.418  1.108


Estimator \widehat{G}_{n}^{a}: \widehat{G}_{n}^{a}= \frac{1}{n\overline{y}}\sum_{i \in S}\{2\widehat{F}_{n}(y_{i})-1\}y_{i}= \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i \in S}\{2\widehat{F}_{n}(y_{i})-1\}y_{i},\qquad T=\sum_{i \in S}y_{i}.

Gn.a <- function(y) {
  FDi <- sapply(y, function(Yi) mean(y <= Yi))
  (1 / sum(y)) * sum((2 * FDi - 1) * y)
}
Gn.a(Y.n)

[1] 0.3803843


Estimator \widehat{G}_{n}^{b}: \widehat{G}_{n}^{b}=\frac{1}{2n^{2}\overline{y}}\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S}|y_{i}-y_{j}|=\frac{1}{2nT}\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S}|y_{i}-y_{j}|.

Gn.b <- function(y) {
  n <- length(y)
  ABSi <- sapply(y, function(Yi) sum(abs(y - Yi)))
  sum(ABSi) / (2 * n * sum(y))
}
Gn.b(Y.n)

[1] 0.3603843


Estimators \widehat{G}_{n}^{b1}, \widehat{G}_{n}^{b2} and \widehat{G}_{n}^{b3} (equivalent expressions of \widehat{G}_{n}^{b} based on the ordered sample y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(n)}): \widehat{G}_{n}^{b1} = \frac{2}{nT}\sum_{i=1}^{n} i\, y_{(i)} - \frac{n+1}{n},\qquad
\widehat{G}_{n}^{b2} = \frac{2\widehat{\beta}}{n} - \frac{n+1}{n},\quad \widehat{\beta}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n} i\,y_{(i)},\qquad
\widehat{G}_{n}^{b3} = \frac{2}{T}\,\mathrm{cov}(i, y_{(i)}).

Gn.b1 <- function(y) { n <- length(y); (2 / (n * sum(y))) * sum((1:n) * sort(y)) - (n + 1) / n }
Gn.b2 <- function(y) { n <- length(y); Beta <- sum((1:n) * sort(y)) / sum(y); 2 * Beta / n - (n + 1) / n }
Gn.b3 <- function(y) { n <- length(y); (2 / sum(y)) * (mean((1:n) * sort(y)) - mean(1:n) * mean(y)) }
c(b1 = Gn.b1(Y.n), b2 = Gn.b2(Y.n), b3 = Gn.b3(Y.n))

       b1        b2        b3 
0.3603843 0.3603843 0.3603843 


Estimator \widehat{G}_{n}^{c} (bias-corrected version): \widehat{G}_{n}^{c}= \frac{n}{n-1}\widehat{G}_{n}^{b}=\frac{1}{2(n-1)T}\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S}|y_{i}-y_{j}|.

Gn.c <- function(y) { n <- length(y); n * Gn.b(y) / (n - 1) }
Gn.c(Y.n)

[1] 0.3677391


Estimators \widehat{G}_{n}^{c1}, \widehat{G}_{n}^{c2} and \widehat{G}_{n}^{c3}: \widehat{G}_{n}^{c1} = \frac{2}{(n-1)T}\sum_{i=1}^{n} i\, y_{(i)} - \frac{n+1}{n-1},\qquad
\widehat{G}_{n}^{c2} = \frac{1}{2\overline{y}}\binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{1 \leq i_{1} < i_{2} \leq n} |y_{i_{1}}-y_{i_{2}}|,\qquad
\widehat{G}_{n}^{c3} = 1 - \frac{\overline{z}}{\overline{y}}, where z_i = (n-1)^{-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\min(y_i,y_j).

Gn.c1 <- function(y) { n <- length(y); (2 / ((n - 1) * sum(y))) * sum((1:n) * sort(y)) - (n + 1) / (n - 1) }
Gn.c2 <- function(y) {
  n <- length(y); pairs <- combn(n, 2)
  (1 / (2 * mean(y))) * sum(abs(y[pairs[1, ]] - y[pairs[2, ]])) / choose(n, 2)
}
Gn.c3 <- function(y) {
  n <- length(y)
  zi <- sapply(1:n, function(i) sum(pmin(y[-i], y[i]))) / (n - 1)
  1 - mean(zi) / mean(y)
}
c(c1 = Gn.c1(Y.n), c2 = Gn.c2(Y.n), c3 = Gn.c3(Y.n))

title: The Gini index: definition and estimation
text:
Estimation in finite populations
A sample of size n=50 is selected by simple random sampling without replacement from a population of size N=10{,}000 generated from a Pareto distribution. The survey weights are w_i = N/n.

set.seed(123)
Y.N <- rpareto_base(n = 10000, shape = 1.5)
Y.n <- sample(Y.N, size = 50)
w.n <- rep(10000 / 50, 50)

Estimator \widehat{G}_{w}^{a}: \widehat{G}_{w}^{a}= \frac{2}{\widehat{N}\overline{y}_{w}}\sum_{i \in S}w_{i}y_{i}\widehat{F}_{w}(y_{i})-1.

Gw.a <- function(y, w) {
  N.Hat <- sum(w)
  FDi <- sapply(y, function(Yi) sum(w * (y <= Yi)) / N.Hat)
  Mean.y <- sum(w * y) / N.Hat
  (2 / (N.Hat * Mean.y)) * sum(w * y * FDi) - 1
}
Gw.a(Y.n, w.n)

[1] 0.3356694


Estimator \widehat{G}_{w}^{b}: \widehat{G}_{w}^{b}=\frac{1}{2\widehat{N}^{2}\overline{y}_{w}}\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S}w_{i}w_{j}|y_{i}-y_{j}|.

Gw.b <- function(y, w) {
  N.Hat <- sum(w)
  ABSi <- sapply(y, function(Yi) sum(w * abs(y - Yi)))
  Mean.y <- sum(w * y) / N.Hat
  sum(w * ABSi) / (2 * N.Hat^2 * Mean.y)
}

title: Gini index calculator
text:
How to interpret the results

\widehat{G}_n^{b} is the usual estimator (equivalently, the Gini index with the mid-point distribution function); \widehat{G}_n^{c} = \frac{n}{n-1}\widehat{G}_n^{b} is its bias-corrected version; \widehat{G}_n^{a} is shown for comparison only: it overestimates inequality when inequality is low.
With sampling weights, the weighted estimator \widehat{G}_{w} (mid-point distribution function) is used.
Jackknife bias: estimated bias of the estimator. With small samples or very skewed data the Gini index is usually underestimated.
Standard error and 95% intervals: precision of the estimate. Differences between groups, regions or years should be interpreted in the light of these margins of error.
With sampling weights, the jackknife and the bootstrap delete or resample one unit at a time and ignore the sampling design (strata, clusters); for complex surveys, use fgini() in giniVarCI.

F.J. García-Martínez, F. Osorio and F. González-Gómez (Water, 2025; JCR Q2). Read the article.
The question. Do people in small villages get the same water services as people in cities?
What they found.

Water management in Spain shows two very different realities: populated areas and small towns.
Small municipalities face specific problems in managing the urban water cycle.
Recommendations: create optimal service areas and an independent regulatory body.

Link with inequality. Territorial inequality: whether you live in a city or a village should not decide the quality of your water service.

title: In one minute: Changing prices after the reform of local public services: remunicipalization versus privatization

D. Albalate, G. Bel, F. González-Gómez, J.C. Hernández-Gutiérrez and A.J. Picazo-Tadeo (Journal of Regulatory Economics, 2024; JCR Q3). Read the article.
The question. When a town takes its water service back from a private company, or hands it over to one, what happens to the water bill?
What they found.

Remunicipalization showed smaller price increases than privatization.
But that gap came from a few towns with abnormally low prices before the reform.
Once these towns are accounted for, the type of reform makes no difference to prices.

Key result (in the video). What happened to water prices after the reform. Source: Journal of Regulatory Economics (2024), Spanish municipalities.

Link with inequality. Water bills weigh more on low-income households. Knowing what drives water prices helps protect affordability and the human right to water.

The question. Does tourism help to reduce poverty and social exclusion in European regions?
What they found.

International (inbound) tourism increases poverty and social exclusion in destination regions.
Domestic tourism reduces them, in destinations and in neighbouring regions.
Some other effects are statistically significant but economically very small.

Key result (in the video). Effect of tourism on the risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE). Source: Economia Politica (2026), EU regions. The inverted-U link of total tourism is negligible in practice.
Why it matters. Tourism does not reduce poverty by itself. Market structures, labour regulation, competitiveness and social protection decide who benefits.

The question. Are young graduates paid differently in Italy and in Germany? And are women paid less than men?

The wage gap against Italian talents grew in 2022, mainly because the same qualifications are paid less.
The gap grew more for women, especially at the top.
Gender gap among talents: Italy from 10% to 22.5%; Germany from 27.5% to 15%.

title: In one minute: A practical guide to proper estimation and inference of the Gini index by avoiding often encountered methodological pitfalls
text:
J.F. Muñoz, J.M. Pavía and E. Álvarez-Verdejo (Social Indicators Research, 2026; JCR Q1). Read the article.
The question. The Gini index is the most used measure of inequality. But computing it from data is error-prone. Do common practices give wrong numbers and wrong margins of error?
What they found.

Some widely used formulas give inaccurate estimates of inequality.
A popular regression-based method seriously underestimates the margin of error when incomes are very skewed and unequal.
Jackknife methods give the most accurate margins of error.

Key result (in the video). How often the 95% margin of error contains the true Gini. Monte Carlo illustration: lognormal incomes, samples of 100, 4,000 replications (computed by GiniUs). As inequality grows, the regression method falls far below 95%.
Why it matters. Margins of error that are too small can make us believe inequality changed when it did not. The paper gives practical recommendations and the free R package giniVarCI.

title: Missing incomes can make inequality look smaller than it is
text:
Income is one of the questions that people most often refuse to answer in surveys. If the people who do not answer were just a random subset of the sample (MCAR), deleting them would only cost precision. But non-response is rarely random: very rich and, sometimes, very poor households answer less often.
When high incomes are more often missing, the respondents look more equal than the population, and the Gini index computed with the complete cases underestimates inequality. Two popular fixes make things worse:

Mean imputation gives every non-respondent the same income, so it removes inequality by construction.
Regression imputation without a random residual places every imputed value on the regression line, with the same effect.

If non-response depends on variables that we observe for everybody, such as education, age or region (MAR), multiple imputation with these variables in the imputation model removes most of the bias and gives honest margins of error. If it depends on income itself (MNAR), no standard method is enough, and sensitivity analyses are needed.
You can see all this with your own eyes in the missing data simulator: choose a distribution, a percentage of missing data and a mechanism, and compare six methods. This is the topic of objective OG2 of GiniUs.

title: In one minute: Exploring and correcting the bias in the estimation of the Gini measure of inequality
text:
J.F. Muñoz, P.J. Moya-Fernández and E. Álvarez-Verdejo (Sociological Methods & Research, 2025; JCR Q1). Read the article.
The question. There are many formulas to estimate the Gini index from a sample. Do they all give the right answer?
What they found.

One popular formula strongly overestimates inequality when inequality is low.
With skewed and unequal data, the usual estimators tend to underestimate inequality.
Bootstrap and jackknife corrections reduce the bias, and a simple criterion tells when to use them.

Key result (in the video). Relative bias (%) of three common Gini formulas. Monte Carlo illustration with the paper’s estimators: lognormal incomes, samples of 20 people, 20,000 replications (computed by GiniUs).
Why it matters. Differences in inequality between countries, regions or groups can come from the formula used, not from real differences. Choosing the right estimator avoids wrong conclusions.

title: In one minute: The “Happy and Poor” paradox: why do some poor people report being very happy?
text:
J. Guardiola, F. García-Quero and A. García-García (Applied Research in Quality of Life, 2026; JCR Q1). Read the article.
The question. Many people living in poverty say they are very happy. How can that be?
Six explanations.

Their basic needs are met and they are satisfied in key areas of life; they adapt to hardship and have modest aspirations.
Scientists and policymakers may misjudge how well they are doing.
Their culture supports happiness, and maldevelopment has not eroded it.

The idea in one picture (in the video). Income and life satisfaction. Conceptual illustration. The study explains why some poor people are in the top-left corner.
Why it matters. Poverty is not only a lack of income. Listening to how people evaluate their own lives helps design better development policies.

title: In one minute: Unconditional variance estimation under complex surveys
text:
Y.G. Berger (International Statistical Review, 2025; JCR Q1). Read the article.
The question. How precise are the figures we get from large official surveys?
What they found.

The margin of error can be computed without complex correction terms.
The estimator is simple and asymptotically unbiased under stratified, multistage and informative designs.
It also gives hypothesis tests and works under ordered systematic sampling.

Key result (in the video). A simpler way to get the margin of error. Source: International Statistical Review (2025).
Why it matters. Simple and reliable margins of error make it easier to use survey data correctly.
Link with inequality. Inequality and poverty are measured with complex surveys such as EU-SILC. Reliable margins of error tell us whether a change in inequality is real.

title: In one minute: Dynamic spatio-temporal modelling of tourism impact on income inequality and polarization: inbound and domestic flows in the EU
text:
C.M. Llorca-Rodríguez, A.C. Casas-Jurado, R.M. García-Fernández and J. Chica-Olmo (Papers in Regional Science, 2025; JCR Q2, ABS 3). Read the article.
The question. Does tourism make income more equal in European regions, or less?
What they found.

Overall, tourism and inequality follow an inverted-U shape.
Inbound tourism increases inequality and polarization in destinations; domestic tourism reduces them.
Both types improve the income distribution of neighbouring regions.

Key result (in the video). Effect of tourism on income inequality and polarization. Source: Papers in Regional Science (2025), EU NUTS-1 regions. Overall, tourism and inequality follow an inverted-U shape.
Why it matters. Useful for the EU Cohesion Policy: domestic tourism supports cohesion, and social protection (education, health, unemployment and retirement) should be strengthened.

title: In one minute: Pro-environmental behaviour in household water use. A gender perspective
text:
L. Granda, P.J. Moya-Fernández, R.M. Soriano-Miras and F. González-Gómez (Sustainable Water Resources Management, 2024). Read the article.
The question. Do women and men save water at home in the same way?
What they found.

There is no gender gap in the number of water-saving habits.
But there are differences in specific habits.
They follow how household chores are shared: tasks traditionally done by women or by men.

Key result (in the video). Saving water at home: women and men. Source: Sustainable Water Resources Management (2024), ten household water uses.
Why it matters. Water-saving campaigns work better when they reach the person who actually does each household task.
Link with inequality. Gender inequality in sharing household chores also shapes who carries the effort of saving water at home.

title: In one minute: Does economic growth drive equitable water and sanitation access? Assessing inequality reduction across 64 nations
text:
M. García-López, S. López-Ruiz and G. Cuadrado-Quesada (Sustainable Development, 2026; JCR Q1). Read the article.
The question. When a country grows richer, does access to water and sanitation become more equal?
What they found.

Growth improves access overall, but the poorest and rural populations are left behind.
Inequality in sanitation is not related to growth.
Unequal access to water also holds back GDP per capita.

Key result (in the video). What economic growth does, and does not do, for water and sanitation. Source: Sustainable Development (2026), 64 countries.
Why it matters. Growth alone will not deliver water and sanitation for all (SDG 6). Effective governance and efficient water use are needed.

title: Research data and R code
text: The simulation studies of GiniUs use samples from continuous distributions frequently used to model incomes: Pareto, Dagum (with shape parameters p=20 and p=0.5), lognormal, Weibull and Gamma. Their parameters are chosen so that the Gini index takes a given value G, which allows the effect of inequality and skewness on the estimators to be studied. All the code fixes the random seed with set.seed(), so every result can be replicated.

GINI.GAMMA <- function(k, GINI) gamma((2 * k + 1) / 2) / (k * gamma(k) * sqrt(pi)) - GINI
GINI.DAGUM <- function(p, GINI, a) gamma(p) * gamma(2 * p + 1 / a) / (gamma(2 * p) * gamma(p + 1 / a)) - 1 - GINI

G <- 0.4
SIGMA.Log <- qnorm((G + 1) / 2) * sqrt(2)
ALPHA.Par <- (1 + G) / (2 * G)
K.Wei     <- 1 / log2(1 / (1 - G))

a.Dag     <- uniroot(GINI.DAGUM, c(0.1, 16), GINI = G, p = 20)$root    # Dagum, p = 20

section: Monte Carlo study of the bias (Figure 2 of the proposal)
text:
Monte Carlo study of the bias (Figure 2 of the proposal)
library(VGAM)
set.seed(2023)
R <- 1000; N <- 50
VECTOR.G <- seq(0.1, 0.8, by = 0.1)

estimators <- function(y) {
  n <- length(y)
  Gb <- (2 / (n * sum(y))) * sum(rank(y) * y) - (n + 1) / n
  c(Ga = Gb + 1 / n, Gb = Gb, Gc = n * Gb / (n - 1))
}
draw <- function(dist, G, n) {
  switch(dist,
    Pareto    = rpareto(n, scale = 1, shape = (1 + G) / (2 * G)),
    Lognormal = rlnorm(n, 5, qnorm((G + 1) / 2) * sqrt(2)),
    Weibull   = rweibull(n, shape = 1 / log2(1 / (1 - G))),
    Gamma     = rgamma(n, shape = uniroot(GINI.GAMMA, c(0.15, 130), GINI = G)$root),
    DagumP20  = rdagum(n, shape1.a = uniroot(GINI.DAGUM, c(0.1, 16), GINI = G, p = 20)$root, shape2.p = 20),
    DagumP05  = rdagum(n, shape1.a = uniroot(GINI.DAGUM, c(0.1, 16), GINI = G, p = 0.5)$root, shape2.p = 0.5))
}
RB <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Pareto", "DagumP20", "DagumP05", "Lognormal", "Weibull", "Gamma"), function(dist)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(VECTOR.G, function(G) {
    est <- replicate(R, estimators(draw(dist, G, N)))
    data.frame(distribution = dist, G = G, t(round(100 * (rowMeans(est) - G) / G, 2)))
  }))))

title: Glossary and FAQ
text:
Gini index

The most widely used measure of inequality, proposed by Corrado Gini (1912). It is 0 under perfect equality (everybody has the same income) and approaches 1 when one person has all the income. It can be read as half the expected absolute difference between the incomes of two people chosen at random, divided by the mean income.

Lorenz curve

Curve that shows the cumulative share of income held by the poorest p\% of the population. The Gini index is twice the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve.

Estimator

Formula that computes the Gini index from a sample. The literature contains many estimators (\widehat{G}_n^{a}, \widehat{G}_n^{b}, \widehat{G}_n^{c}, …), which give different results in the same sample; see Definition and estimation.

Infinite and finite populations

In the infinite-population (model-based) approach, data are independent draws from a distribution. In the finite-population (design-based) approach, data come from a sample survey with sampling weights w_i, and the target is the Gini index of the finite population.

Bias of an estimator

Difference between the average value of an estimator over all possible samples and the true value. Gini estimators can be biased upwards (\widehat{G}_n^{a} with low inequality) or downwards (highly skewed and unequal data).

Relative bias (RB)

Bias divided by the true value, in percent. In GiniUs: negligible if |RB|<2\%, acceptable if |RB|<5\%, and large otherwise.

Skewness

Asymmetry of a distribution. Incomes have a long right tail: few people with very high values. The project shows that skewness and inequality affect the bias of the Gini estimators.

Jackknife

Resampling method that recomputes the estimator leaving out one observation at a time, to estimate its bias and variance.

Bootstrap

Resampling method that draws many samples with replacement from the data to approximate the distribution of an estimator and build confidence intervals. The rescaled bootstrap adapts it to finite populations, and the empirical bootstrap is used to correct biases.

Linearisation

Approximation of the variance of an estimator by a first-order Taylor expansion (influence functions).

Empirical likelihood

Non-parametric method that builds confidence intervals without assuming a distribution, with good coverage for the Gini index.

Confidence interval and coverage

Range of values that contains the true value with a given probability (e.g. 95%). An interval has good coverage when that probability is achieved in practice.

Missing data, non-response

Values that should have been observed but were not, for example because a person refused to report his or her income.

MCAR, MAR and MNAR

Response mechanisms (Rubin, 1976). MCAR: the probability of non-response is the same for everybody. MAR: it depends only on observed variables. MNAR: it depends on the unobserved value itself (e.g. high incomes are less often reported). See the missing data simulator.

Complete-case analysis

Deleting the units with missing values. It is unbiased only under MCAR and always loses precision.

Single and multiple imputation

Replacing each missing value with one (single) or several (multiple) plausible values. Multiple imputation repeats the imputation M times and combines the results with Rubin’s rules, so that the uncertainty due to imputation is reflected in the variance.

title: Glossary and FAQ
text:
Frequently asked questions
Which estimator of the Gini index should I use? It depends on the data. With samples without weights, \widehat{G}_n^{c}=\frac{n}{n-1}\widehat{G}_n^{b} corrects most of the bias of the usual estimator in symmetric or moderately skewed data; \widehat{G}_n^{a} should be avoided when inequality is low. With highly skewed data and small samples, a bias correction (e.g. jackknife) is advisable. With survey data, use the weighted estimators. The articles of the project explain the choice in detail.
Is the bias important in practice? It can be. With small samples, small groups or highly skewed distributions, the relative bias of the usual estimators can exceed 10%. Try the bias explorer or the calculator.
How can I obtain a margin of error for my Gini index? With the jackknife, the bootstrap, linearisation or empirical likelihood, all available in the R package giniVarCI. The calculator gives jackknife and bootstrap intervals in your browser.
Can the Gini index be computed with zero or negative incomes? Zero incomes are allowed. With negative incomes the Gini index can exceed 1 and loses its usual interpretation; they should be treated explicitly and reported.
Can the Gini index be decomposed by groups? Not additively: the Gini index of a population is not the sum of a between-group and a within-group term (there is a residual overlap term). Theil indices can be decomposed exactly; see the follow-up project THEILUMINA.
My survey has missing incomes. What should I do? Report the percentage of missing data, analyse the response mechanism, avoid mean imputation and complete-case analysis unless the data are MCAR, and use multiple imputation with an imputation model that includes the variables related to income and to non-response. See the missing data simulator.
Where can I find official data on inequality? In the observatory (Eurostat, World Bank and INE) and in the links of interest.
Is there an easy way to learn about your results without reading the articles? Yes. Our one-minute videos explain the articles on inequality and poverty in plain language, and the blog publishes short posts on our work.
Can I use the materials of this website in my classes? Yes, citing the source as indicated in How to cite. This includes the one-minute videos.

title: Missing data simulator
text: Missing data are very common in inequality studies: people are less willing to answer sensitive questions such as their income, and those who do not answer are often different from those who do. This simulator, linked to objective OG2 of the project, shows how much the Gini index can be biased by missing data, depending on the response mechanism and on the method used to deal with the missing values. It runs a Monte Carlo experiment in your browser.

title: Missing data simulator
text:
The three response mechanisms


MCAR · Missing completely at randomThe probability of non-response is the same for everybody. The respondents are a random subsample of the sample.


MAR · Missing at randomNon-response depends on an observed variable x (for example, education, age or occupation) that is related to income, but not on income itself once x is known.


MNAR · Missing not at randomNon-response depends on the income itself: for example, people with very high (or very low) incomes are less willing to report it.


In the simulation, the probability that unit i does not respond follows a logistic model P(\text{missing}_i)=\{1+\exp(-\alpha-\beta\,v_i)\}^{-1}, where v_i=0 under MCAR, v_i=x_i under MAR and v_i is the (standardised) rank of y_i under MNAR. The intercept \alpha is set so that the expected percentage of missing data is the one chosen, and \beta is the strength of the mechanism. The auxiliary variable x is observed for everybody and its correlation with the (normal scores of) income is \rho.

How to read the results




Complete cases (deleting the units with missing data) is only safe under MCAR. Under MAR and MNAR the respondents are no longer representative, and if the richest people do not respond, inequality is underestimated.
Mean imputation always underestimates inequality, because all the imputed incomes are equal. It should never be used to estimate the Gini index.
Regression imputation also underestimates inequality, because it ignores the residual variability of income.
Stochastic regression imputation and multiple imputation add a random residual to the prediction. Under MAR, they remove most of the bias, provided that the imputation model includes the variable x that explains non-response. Multiple imputation also reflects the uncertainty due to imputation and has a smaller error.
Under MNAR, no standard method removes the bias. Sensitivity analyses and auxiliary information on the non-respondents are needed.
Increase the percentage of missing data, the strength of the mechanism or the inequality of the data to see how the problems grow; reduce the correlation \rho to see how imputation loses its advantage under MAR.

Method
What it does

Complete cases

MCAR (or within classes that explain non-response)

Predicts \log y from x with a linear regression fitted to the respondents
Not for inequality measures (ignores residual variability)

Prediction plus a residual drawn at random from the respondents’ residuals

Stochastic regression repeated M times, refitting the model on bootstrap samples of the respondents; the M Gini indices are averaged (Rubin’s rules)

Good practice when estimating the Gini index with missing data. Report the percentage of missing data and analyse the response mechanism; never use mean imputation or simply delete the incomplete cases unless the data are MCAR; include in the imputation model the variables related to income and to non-response; use multiple imputation with enough imputations for the percentage of missing data; and report the uncertainty due to imputation.



The code of the simulator is in js/gini-sim.js. Estimator of the Gini index: \widehat{G}_n^{c}. Gamma is not included because the simulator generates the income and the auxiliary variable through a normal copula, which requires a closed-form quantile function.

title: Research problems and questions
text:
Inequality is a source of conflict in society, and its measurement is essential to respond to the social and economic concerns of citizens. Recent events (the 2008 financial crisis, COVID-19, inflation, rising energy costs and interest rates) increase the risk of widening inequality. To have a realistic view of inequality and design corrective policies, measurements must be reliable, without biases or errors: a large bias can lead to invalid inferences and wrong conclusions (Särndal et al., 2003).
The Gini index (G) is the most popular inequality indicator. It is easy to interpret (0 means perfect equality and 1 maximum inequality) and allows comparisons between countries, regions or groups (by sex, age, etc.). The project identifies and quantifies four problems, formulates eleven research questions and tests two hypotheses that had not been investigated in the literature.

title: Research problems and questions
text:
Theoretical framework
Let Y be a continuous, non-negative variable (e.g. income) with mean \mu and distribution function F(y). The most popular formulations of the Gini index are (Berger and Gedik, 2020):

G = \frac{1}{\mu}\int \{2F(y)-1\}\,y\,dF(y) = \frac{1}{2\mu}\iint |x-y|\,dF(x)\,dF(y).

In practice, G is estimated from a sample S of size n. There is a great controversy about which empirical version should be used, because the many available expressions give different results (Giorgi and Gigliarano, 2017). The three most common estimators are

\widehat{G}_n^{a} = \frac{2}{n\bar{y}}\sum_{i\in S} y_i\widehat{F}_n(y_i) - 1, \qquad
\widehat{G}_n^{b} = \frac{1}{2n^2\bar{y}}\sum_{i\in S}\sum_{j\in S}|y_i-y_j|, \qquad
\widehat{G}_n^{c} = \frac{n}{n-1}\,\widehat{G}_n^{b},

where \widehat{G}_n^{c} is frequently used to reduce the bias of \widehat{G}_n^{b}. All the expressions are listed on the page Definition and estimation.

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 1. Large biases in the estimation of the Gini index
text:
Problem 1. Large biases in the estimation of the Gini index

Question 1. Is there an exhaustive review that collects all the expressions of the Gini index and establishes the relationships among them?
Question 2. Which expression of the Gini index should be used, given the data available in an empirical study of inequality?
Question 3. Can characteristics of the data, such as skewness or inequality, affect the bias of the Gini estimators?

No reference collects and relates all the expressions of the Gini index; Giorgi and Gigliarano (2017) ignore finite populations and estimators such as \widehat{G}_n^{c}. Previous studies on the bias (Deltas, 2003; Davidson, 2009; Berger and Gedik, 2020) analyse a single estimator with data of similar inequality and skewness. The project tests two new hypotheses:

H1. The skewness of the data affects the bias of the Gini estimators.
H2. The inequality of the data affects the bias of the Gini estimators.

A Monte Carlo study with 48 scenarios (Pareto, Dagum with p=20 and p=0.5, lognormal, Weibull and Gamma distributions, with G = 0.1,\ldots,0.8 and n=50) showed that:

\widehat{G}_n^{a} has excessively large biases with low inequality;
skewness has an important effect on the bias of the three estimators;
in highly skewed distributions, inequality also has an important effect on the bias.

The bias is considered negligible when |RB| < 2\%, acceptable when |RB| < 5\%, and large otherwise, where RB = 100\times\{E(\widehat{G})-G\}/G is the relative bias. You can reproduce and extend this study with the interactive bias explorer.

Question 4. Which methods should be applied to reduce this bias?
Question 5. Can a criterion be established to help institutions and researchers know when their data may have large biases, so that correction techniques must be applied?

The project investigates the bootstrap (including the rescaled bootstrap; Berger and Muñoz, 2015; Muñoz et al., 2018; Moya et al., 2023), the jackknife (Berger and Skinner, 2005; Berger, 2008) and the empirical bootstrap (Pfeffermann and Correa, 2012), and a practical criterion based on the relative bias, the bias ratio and the mean squared error.

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 2. Missing data and the Gini index
text:
Problem 2. Missing data and the Gini index

Question 6. What are the consequences of missing data for the estimation of the Gini index?
Question 7. What is the best strategy to deal with missing data in studies based on the Gini index, so that estimates are precise, robust and reliable?

The consequences of missing data (non-response bias, larger variance, distortion of the relationships between variables) have not been exhaustively investigated for the Gini index. The most common solution is to replace each missing value by one (single imputation) or several (multiple imputation) plausible values (Van Buuren, 2018; Muñoz and Rueda, 2009). Studies on inequality measures have important limitations: they do not compare imputation techniques, ignore the effect of skewness and inequality, and ignore the type of non-response mechanism. Missing data are very likely because people are less willing to answer sensitive questions such as income, which generates larger non-response bias. The missing data simulator illustrates the problem under the three mechanisms (MCAR, MAR and MNAR).

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 3. Lack of software for the Gini index
text:
Problem 3. Lack of software for the Gini index

Question 8. Is there software that computes the different expressions of the Gini index, their variances and confidence intervals with all the methods available in the literature?

When the project started, R packages such as DescTools and laeken did not estimate the variance and only provided bootstrap intervals; ineq, reldist, GiniWegNeg and dineq only computed point estimates. Stata (fastgini, ineqdeco, ineqerr), SPSS and SAS had similar limitations. Other methods (jackknife, linearisation, empirical likelihood) can be more accurate (Berger, 2008; Berger and Gedik, 2020). This problem has been solved with the R package giniVarCI.

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 4. Applications in the Social Sciences
text:
Problem 4. Applications in the Social Sciences

Question 9. What are the applications of the Gini index, and which techniques are used to deal with missing data, in the research areas of the members of the project?
Question 10. Do inequality studies in these areas use the optimal expression of the Gini index and confidence intervals with desirable properties?
Question 11. Do inequality studies with missing information in these areas deal with missing data with the required scientific rigour?

The review of the literature found studies on water that use multiple imputation with 50% missing data without reporting the imputation model or checking its assumptions, or that impute with the mean; studies in strategic management and international business (some in ABS 4* and 4 journals) that use five imputations with 23% missing data or ignore the non-response mechanism with 75% missing data; and studies on tourism and inequality that simply delete the cases with missing data. Some do not use the unbiased version of the Gini index, so bias is a serious problem with small samples or highly skewed data. The project prepares methodological contributions for each area that explain how to detect and avoid these biases and errors.
